summary: A Green Mountain Technologies blog post on keeping compost piles moist in hot, dry climates. It argues that microbes need adequate moisture and recommends shading piles, applying a thick biocover layer, avoiding overly dry feedstocks, following specific watering practices, and using aeration strategies to manage heat and moisture. The surrounding navigation menus, footers and social links are site boilerplate and were ignored.
one_line: Green Mountain Technologies blog on strategies for conserving moisture in compost piles in hot, dry climates through shading, biocover, watering and aeration.
key_facts: Without adequate moisture, compost microbes cannot survive, and an overly dry compost pile will experience a huge loss of microbial diversity.
An overly dry compost pile will be unable to maintain internally-generated composting temperatures of 120-140 deg F.
Biocover feedstocks typically have a particle size of 4-6" or larger with a significant amount of fiber, such as wood chips, leaves, weeds or straw.
A thick layer of at least 6-12" of biocover material is beneficial over all compost piles.
Feedstocks that become overly dry tend to become hydrophobic and resist absorbing water, so added water tends to run off.
Pre-watering feedstocks, for example with a sub-surface drip irrigation system, increases contact time to absorb water and rehydrate.
Feedstocks with embodied water, such as food waste or fresh cut green waste, can help boost the moisture content of the overall mixture.
The article recommends a minimum moisture content of 50% to support a hot compost process.
A hot compost pile can easily lose 1% of moisture content every day.
In warm climates, the article recommends a starting moisture content of 60% for a blended compost recipe, providing about 7-10 days before rewetting is needed.

Watering best practices include adding water at least once per week, adding it slowly over longer durations, installing drip irrigation below the pile surface, and watering during cool hours such as evening.
Heat generated by microbial metabolic activity rises through the pile, so the hottest temperatures reside on top of the pile.
For positively-aerated systems, the air going into compost piles can be misted to add moisture and support evaporative cooling.
Negative aeration can induce moisture to condense in lower parts of the pile and allow heat to be dumped into the thermal mass of underground piping.
